newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica forex control may see court challenge-Absa.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica forex control may see court challenge-Absa.

text.p: South Africa's exchange control regulations, which prohibit residents from investing abroad, may soon be challenged in the country's highest court, Amalgamated Banks of South Africa Ltd said on Friday.
Absa said in its latest economic review that certain aspects relating to the enforcement of foreign exchange control measures could already be in conflict with the new constitution.
These included exchange control authorities' right to enter premises without a search warrant, which police are prohibited from doing.

"This right of the authorities can be argued as being incompatible with the 'right to privacy' provisions incorporated in the new constitution, and could therefore be challenged in the Constitutional Court," Absa said.

Authorities' right to interrogate people suspected of infringing forex control laws, where a refusal to reply is regarded as a contravention, appeared to be in conflict with the constitution's "right to remain silent" premise, the bank said.
"Thirdly, the whole apparatus of exchange controls could be challenged on the grounds that they infringe on human rights, which are a key aspect of the constitution."
Assuming that a court challenge did not settle the issue, Absa listed a number of next possible steps in the further relaxing of exchange regulations.

It rejected a wholesale or "big bang" abolition approach saying South Africa's financial sector was ill prepared for foreign competition and that the country's supervisory environment may need to be changed.

Central Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals last week told a financial conference that government aimed to test demand for the withdrawal of funds from the country by gradually relaxing capital restrictions.
He said that the next step could include private individuals for the first time, but he stressed that any moves would not be spectacular.
Absa said on Friday the scrapping of controls on residents would be a far trickier and longer process than that of non-residents due to locals' pent up desire to take capital abroad.
"High levels of taxation and crime, currency weakness and lingering political uncertainties continue to encourage the outward movement of funds," it said.
Asked last week what kind of pent-up demand there was in South Africa, Stals said around 60 billion rand would "not be unreasonable".
Absa said on Friday blocked rand funds -- money owned by emigrants who had to leave funds in South Africa -- was generally assumed to stand at between 10 and 20 billion rand.

Other control easings might include more concessions for investment in Southern African Development Community member countries, namely Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi and Botswana.

Further concessions could be granted to financial institutions to invest larger portions of their funds abroad, Absa said. Institutions can already invest 10 percent of their total assets offshore in the form asset swaps.

Another step could be the establishment of an investment pool from which financial institutions and individuals could make portfolio investments abroad at a less favourable exchange rate than that of the rand.
Residents could also be allowed to invest abroad through a South African bank which would hold dollars on the client's behalf.
